sections.text: A sleep cycle calculator picks a bedtime so that your alarm falls at the end of a block of 90 minute cycles. For a 6:30 AM alarm, five cycles plus 14 minutes to fall asleep puts the bedtime at 10:46 PM, and six cycles puts it at 9:16 PM. The 90 minute length is a convention that the calculator uses as an approximation, not a measurement of your own sleep, so treat the output as a starting point for a schedule rather than a precise prediction.

The formula is simple. Bedtime = wake time - (number of cycles x 90 minutes) - 14 minutes. The 14 minutes is a fixed allowance for falling asleep. Everything is done in minutes after midnight, and the result wraps around the 24 hour clock. For the other direction, wake time = bedtime + 14 minutes + (cycles x 90 minutes).

Why 90 minutes? It is a commonly used average for the length of one pass through the stages of sleep. Individual cycles vary from person to person and from night to night, and the calculator does not measure them. Nothing in the arithmetic knows your actual sleep.
Here are the four options the calculator lists for two alarm times. The last column is the total time in bed, including the 14 minute allowance.

The calculator lists these from six cycles down to three. Its highlighted recommendation is the first row that has five or six cycles, which in practice is the six cycle row. That is a rule inside the tool, not advice about your needs, so read the whole table and choose the row that matches the sleep you want.
If you already know when you will be in bed, run it the other way. Getting into bed at 11:00 PM gives these wake times:
Only the first two are realistic for most mornings. The point of the exercise is to see how late a given bedtime pushes the earliest sensible alarm.
Because the model fixes two numbers, small differences in your real sleep move the result. Both effects below are straightforward arithmetic on the 10:46 PM, five cycle plan for a 6:30 AM alarm:

items: If you fall asleep in 5 minutes instead of 14, five cycles end at 6:21 AM instead of 6:30. If it takes 30 minutes, they end at 6:46 AM.
If your cycles are 80 minutes instead of 90, five cycles end 50 minutes early. If they are 100 minutes, they end 50 minutes late. The calculator has no way to know which applies to you.

sections.text: This is why a rigid schedule built on the 90 minute number can be wrong by half an hour or more. Using the output as a guide and then adjusting according to how you actually feel is more sensible than following it to the minute.
How much sleep to aim for

Cycle counts and sleep needs are separate questions. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says adults aged 18 to 60 need 7 or more hours of sleep a day. Five cycles (7.5 hours) and six cycles (9.0 hours) in the table above meet that, while four cycles (6.0 hours) and three cycles (4.5 hours) fall below it. Needs differ by age and health, so check the current guidance for your situation instead of relying on a cycle count.

items: Treating 90 minutes and 14 minutes as facts about you. They are modelling assumptions.
Entering the time you start winding down as your bedtime, when the calculation expects the time you get into bed.
Counting time spent awake on a phone in bed as part of the 14 minutes.
Cutting down to four or three cycles on a regular basis because the arithmetic looks tidy.
Changing the alarm to match a cycle boundary while ignoring the total hours, which matter more.

sections.text: The method assumes regular sleep at night. Shift work, jet lag, a baby that wakes you, medication that affects sleep, and conditions that disrupt sleep can all make the model a poor fit. If you wake unrefreshed despite enough time in bed, snore loudly, or feel sleepy during the day, talk to a doctor or other qualified clinician rather than adjusting a schedule.
This guide offers scheduling arithmetic only. It is not medical advice and the calculator cannot diagnose or treat any sleep problem.

sections.heading: Find Your Perfect Bedtime
sections.body: Use TheCalcUniverse Sleep Cycle Calculator to calculate your optimal bedtime or wake-up time based on real sleep science. No guesswork, just better mornings.
